01

What counts as low back pain?

Low back pain (LBP) is pain, muscle tension, or stiffness below the costal margin and above the inferior gluteal folds, with or without leg pain. The lecture distinguishes acute (<3 months), recurrent (acute symptoms that return), and chronic (>3 months).

Why this lecture matters

The speaker frames LBP as a major cause of disability, lost work, health spending, and potential overexposure to opioids. The practical response is safe triage plus active, nonpharmacologic treatment whenever appropriate.

Six lecture objectives

Classify patients; distinguish medical vs PT triage; interpret age-related imaging findings; screen yellow flags; counsel acute and chronic cases; identify who should be referred to PT.

Lecture message: Do not use a structural diagnosis as a shortcut for explaining every episode of back pain. Evaluate the person and triage first.
02

The biopsychosocial examination

PT begins with a subjective interview and an objective examination. The interview explores symptoms, limitations, beliefs, activity, work, mood, coping, sleep, and social context. The exam assesses movement patterns, range of motion, strength, posture/ergonomics, and spinal segmental movement.

The lecture stresses a minimal emphasis on pathoanatomic labeling for uncomplicated, nonspecific LBP.

Biological factors matter, but psychological and social factors can alter pain, disability, and recovery. Screening them is standard triage, not a claim that pain is imaginary.
03

First decision: red flags vs yellow flags

Red flags → medical management

Findings that warrant medical evaluation because serious pathology or rehabilitation-incompatible conditions may be present. The lecture’s TUNA FISH table includes trauma, unexplained weight loss, neurologic findings, age >50, fever, intravenous drug use, steroid use, and history of cancer. Red flags require clinical interpretation; no individual item automatically establishes a diagnosis.

Progressively worsening neurologic deficits belong in the medical lane.

Yellow flags → psychosocial risk management

Beliefs that pain/activity are harmful; depressed mood, social withdrawal, fear/avoidance, poor coping, low social support, compensation/prolonged sick leave, and exaggerated illness behavior. Other factors highlighted include anxiety, smoking, obesity, intense pain, and demanding labor.

Yellow flags affect education, rehabilitation strategy, and sometimes mental-health referral; they are not automatically contraindications to PT.

Important lecture distinction: Leg pain with neurologic findings (e.g., stable radiculopathy or stenosis) is not always a red flag. Progressive neurologic deficits change management.
04

Yellow-flag questionnaires & clinical implications

The slides list PHQ-9, TSK, FABQ, PASS-20, PCS, STarT Back, OSPRO-YF, and Örebro as screening tools. They assess domains including mood, fear of movement, fear-avoidance, pain anxiety, pain catastrophizing, and broader risk of prolonged disability.

ToolCommon screening target
PHQ-9Depressive symptoms
TSKKinesiophobia / fear of movement
FABQFear-avoidance beliefs, including work and activity
PCSCatastrophizing thoughts about pain
PASS-20Pain-related anxiety
STarT Back / OSPRO-YF / ÖrebroStratified psychosocial risk of persistent disability

PTs do not replace psychologists; education, graded rehabilitation, and referrals can address identified barriers. The slides emphasize that pain experience is influenced by the nervous system and context, not dictated exclusively by tissue condition.

05

Treatment-based classification & management lanes

The lecture juxtaposes medical diagnostic triage and PT treatment-based triage. Medical triage asks whether there is serious spinal disease, radicular pain/claudication, or nonspecific LBP. PT triage asks what level of management and rehabilitation is appropriate.

Management laneLecture criteriaNext step
Medical managementRed flags; major medical comorbidity precluding rehab; leg pain with progressive neurologic deficitsMedical workup and/or urgent referral as warranted
Rehabilitation managementMedium–high psychosocial risk; low risk with predominantly leg pain; or minor/controlled comorbidityPT/active rehabilitation, education, risk-modified care
Self-care managementLow psychosocial risk, predominantly axial back pain, minor/controlled conditionsEducation, stay active, monitor response; reassess if persistent/worsening
The lecture advocates PT when no red flags are present, while the TBC algorithm also recognizes a low-risk self-care pathway. These are compatible when individualized to patient risk and preference.
06

Acute versus persistent pain education

Discuss prognosis, safe movement, and the difference between pain intensity and tissue damage. With uncomplicated acute LBP, encourage activity as tolerated; do not prescribe prolonged bed rest. Avoid catastrophic terms that can increase fear; use reassuring, accurate explanations without dismissing symptoms.

The speaker highlights POLICE, prevalence, pain, prognosis, movement, and imaging as educational topics. For chronic LBP, explain that persistent pain may involve neuroplastic changes and altered processing; pain need not imply ongoing tissue injury.

Precision: "Pain is not tissue-dependent" is the speaker’s shorthand for the complex biology of pain—not that tissue pathology is irrelevant. The clinical task is still to assess symptoms and detect serious conditions.
07

Imaging: degeneration does not equal symptoms

The lecture’s central imaging message is that degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic people and increase with age. A radiology report cannot be interpreted without exam findings and a clinical question.

Finding in asymptomatic peopleAge 20Age 40Age 60Age 80
Disk degeneration37%68%88%96%
Disk signal loss17%54%86%97%
Disk height loss24%45%67%84%
Disk bulge30%50%69%84%
Disk protrusion29%33%38%43%

Values reproduced from the Brinjikji et al. 2015 prevalence table shown on lecture slide 35. Values describe asymptomatic groups, not an individual patient's probability of pain.

Exam application: Do not reflexively attribute pain to an age-related “degenerative disc” MRI finding. Match imaging to red flags, physical examination, and suspected pathology.
08

What PT actually does & when to refer

Interventions cited: education, physical activity, manual therapy, and specific exercise. The lecture promotes PT as a nonopioid option and emphasizes collaboration between physician and physical therapist. In chronic cases, consider additional mental-health support when yellow flags are prominent.

Uncomplicated acute LBP

  • Screen for red flags.
  • Assess neurologic findings for progression.
  • Educate about favorable course and activity.
  • Consider PT; avoid routine bed rest.

Persistent or high-risk LBP

  • Screen for yellow flags and disability risk.
  • Use graded activity and individualized PT.
  • Collaborate with mental-health professionals as indicated.
  • Reassess if new concerning symptoms emerge.
09

Source case: 52-year-old with back and hip pain

History: One week of unilateral right low back/gluteal ache (5/10) after strenuous exercise, shooting into posterior thigh. No numbness, weakness, fever, chills, weight loss, or recent infection.

Examination: Normal vitals and gait; painful reduction in lumbar flexion, extension, right sidebending; localized right L5 tenderness. Dermatomes and myotomes L2–S1 normal and symmetric; patellar/Achilles reflexes 2+; no clonus.

Best lecture-aligned plan: Without identified red flags or progressive deficits, explain favorable prognosis, encourage activity as tolerated, and refer to PT as appropriate. Emergency MRI or prolonged bed rest is not supported by this case.

10

Exam-ready integration

Five essential separations

  1. Stable radicular symptoms ≠ progressive neurologic deficit.
  2. Red flags → medical triage; yellow flags → psychosocial-informed rehab.
  3. Age-related imaging abnormality ≠ demonstrated pain generator.
  4. Acute pain ≠ mandatory rest.
  5. Chronic pain ≠ proof of unhealed injury.

Rapid recall

  1. Define the three duration categories.
  2. List five yellow-flag screening instruments.
  3. Name the three management lanes.
  4. Recall disk degeneration in symptom-free patients at 20 vs 80.
  5. Identify the two source-case recommendations ruled out.
